abstract: Autophagy is a central mechanism that promotes stress acclimation and nutrient recycling, thereby contributing to metabolic homeostasis. However, how photosynthetic carbon assimilation is integrated with autophagy remains poorly understood. Here, we establish a functional link between carbon fixation, redox signaling, and autophagy in the green microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Pharmacological inhibition of phosphoribulokinase (PRK), a key enzyme of the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle, induced chloroplast stress, reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and autophagic flux specifically in the light. Consistently, genetic loss of PRK caused light-dependent ROS accumulation and autophagy activation, which was enhanced by carbon limitation and attenuated by ROS scavenging. To determine the physiological relevance of this response, we generated an atg8 knockout mutant and an atg8 prk double mutant. Loss of ATG8 increased ROS accumulation, photosynthetic dysfunction, and cell death when carbon fixation was inhibited, supporting a protective role for autophagy against light-driven metabolic stress. Although both prk and atg8 prk cells were unable to grow under high light, only prk cells resumed growth after transfer to permissive conditions, indicating that autophagy contributes to recovery from prolonged impairment of photosynthetic carbon metabolism. Our findings identify autophagy as a component of the regulatory network linking photosynthetic carbon assimilation with redox homeostasis and cellular acclimation to light stress.
